study.title: Matthew 21 The King's Entry, the Judgment on Sterility and Rejection of the Leaderships
study.overview: Matthew 21 shows Jesus' public arrival to Jerusalem as a meek and promised King, followed by acts revealing his authority over the temple, over religion without fruit and on the leaders of Israel themselves. The chapter advances in tension: the crowd acclaims him, he purifies the temple, teaches with signs and parables, and ends with the religious leaders recognizing that his words condemned them, but still wanting to arrest him. The dominant theme is that the presence of the Kingdom requires a true answer: faith, repentance and fruit, not only religious appearance.

outline.title: The Messianic entrance to Jerusalem
outline.explanation: Jesus organizes the entrance intentionally, fulfilling the Scriptures and presenting himself as the expected King, but coming with meekness and not with military display. The crowd greets him with Messianic language, but still identifies him incompletely.

outline.title: The cleansed temple and the praise of children
outline.explanation: In expelling the sellers, Jesus judges the corruption of the cult and claims the temple as a house of prayer. Then he heals the needy in and defends the praise of the children, showing that true worship recognizes his messianic identity.

outline.title: The fig tree without fruit and the faith that prays
outline.explanation: The fig tree, full of leaves but without fruit, becomes a sign of judgment on an arelative and empty religiosity. Jesus then teaches that faith, without doubt, expressed in prayer, shares in the power of God; the lesson is not curiosity about miracles, but obedient trust.

outline.title: Disposed authority, two children and the rejected vines
outline.explanation: The leaders try to arrest Jesus for the question of authority, but he exposes them for the answer they refuse to give about John. The parables of the two sons and the vineyard show that obeying truth is worth more than promising, and that the leaders rejected the Son, so the kingdom would be taken away from them and given to a fruitful people.

study.context: The chapter begins with Jesus" approach to Jerusalem, on the Mount of Olives, and with its public entry into the city, which marks the beginning of the final stage of his ministry in Matthew. The note provided about Bethfagé only informs that the name is Hebrew and that the place was probably on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, between Bethany and Jerusalem; it is not necessary to go beyond that. The rest of the chapter takes place between Jerusalem, the temple and Bethany, highlighting the direct confrontation between Jesus and the religious authorities.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter unites royalty, judgment and mercy. Jesus is the promised King, but his way of reigning is humble and submissive to God's plan. By purifying the temple, he shows that God does not accept worship mixed with exploitation and profanation. In healing blind and lame, he manifests restoration in the midst of the sacred space. The fig tree and the parable of the vineyard teach that God seeks real fruit, not only leaves, speech or position. The rejection of the leaders does not nullify the Kingdom; on the contrary, it reveals that it will be given over to a people that bears its fruit. The rejected stone that becomes the main indicates that the apparent defeat of Jesus is part of the divine purpose and his exaltation.

scholarViews.insight: The entry of Jesus into Jerusalem begins the section in which the death and resurrection of the Messiah establish salvation, linking this moment to the outcome of the gospel.

The parable of the farmers points to the religious leaders who reject the Son; the application of history lies with the priests and Pharisees as responsible for the refusal of the messenger and the heir.

questions: What changes in our reading of Jesus when we see him entering Jerusalem as a meek King, and not as a leader of human power?
Is there in our lives external religious signs, such as leaves in the fig tree, but little real fruit of repentance, justice, and obedience?
Will we answer God only with correct words, or also with actions that confirm our faith?
study.practice: This chapter calls the believer to receive Jesus with humility and reverence, to examine whether his religiosity produces true fruit and to treat God's house with seriousness, without turning worship into consumption or appearance. In practice, this means praying with faith, repenting where there is spiritual sterility, obeying what Christ has already revealed and welcoming his authority even when he confronts our interests. It also warns us not to confuse momentary acclaim with persevering fidelity.
study.uncertainty: This site has a likely location only and an etymological explanation suggested; therefore, this data should be treated with caution. The applications on the fig tree and the vineyard follow the interpretive reading provided in the notes; other Christian readings can emphasize different nuances, although the text clearly points to judgment on unbelief and sterility. The gospel of Matthew here does not detail all the later developments of these images, so some theological connections are responsible inferences, not explicit statements of the verse.
